item.content:encoded:
By Evan Woodbery, mlive.com
DETROIT — Scott Harris didn’t have to spend much time searching for the stretch that doomed the Detroit Tigers’ season.
That miserable May is right there for everyone to see.
The Tigers went 6-22, tumbled into last place in the American League Central and spent the rest of the summer trying to recover. They never really did, finishing 76-86 and missing the postseason for the first time in three years.
Less than 24 hours after the season ended, Harris offered his explanation for how a team that entered the year with championship aspirations wound up 10 games under .500.
“This season, and the fact that we’re sitting here right now, is a missed opportunity for this organization, plain and simple,” the Tigers’ president of baseball operations said Monday at Comerica Park. “We’ve got to get better.”
Some of those explanations are easier to quantify than others. Here’s Harris’ assessment of what went wrong.
The May meltdown
There are a lot of ways to dissect a 162-game season, but the brutal 28-game stretch early in the season was a gut punch to the Tigers’ plans to contend in 2026.
“There are a lot of reasons why we’re sitting here and not in the playoffs right now,” Harris said. “One of them really sticks out above the rest for me. You can’t go 6-22 in a month and expect to punch your ticket to the postseason at this level.”
“I think one of the things that I’m really struggling to process about this year is, in many ways, this roster performed quite well for five months, excluding May.”
Before and after May, the Tigers went 70-64. Even more notably, Harris said, they ranked second in baseball in team ERA, second in wRC+ (weighted runs created plus) and posted a plus-119 run differential.
“That’s playoff-worthy. If anything, our record probably should have been even better than 70-64, given the underlying run production and run prevention.”
Why did May happen?
Harris’ answer began with injuries.
Injuries, and a roster that couldn’t absorb them
The Tigers were hit unusually hard by injuries.
Second baseman Gleyber Torres, outfielder Kerry Carpenter, reliever Will Vest and, of course, ace starter Tarik Skubal missed most or all of the month.
Even without Skubal and Vest, run prevention generally wasn’t the biggest problem. The lineup cratered, with significant at-bats going to fill-ins like Gage Workman and Zack Short. Role players like Jahmai Jones, Zach McKinstry and Matt Vierling were pressed into larger roles while mired in prolonged slumps.
“Our roster never really saw the light of day,” Harris said. “We built a roster that we thought was talented, that many people in this room thought was really talented, and they never all actually got on the field at the same time.”
“It’s really hard to have an honest conversation about this organization in the 2026 season without noting that we put 41 players on the injured list on our 40-man roster this year,” Harris said.
“It’s not an excuse. But at some point, you get to a volume of injuries that becomes destabilizing to your ability to manage a roster. I think it did. It really hurt us in certain sections of this year.”
But Harris also said he didn’t build enough depth beyond the active roster to handle what happened.
“Upon reflection, our inability to overcome adversity in real time starts with me,” Harris said. “I didn’t build enough depth into this roster this year. The vulnerabilities in this roster got exposed in May, and it cost us.”
Harris said Detroit entered the season knowing it would become deeper as the summer progressed, with prospects like center fielder Max Clark slated to arrive later.
“I think the main mistake that I made was our depth was coming a little bit too late, basically in all facets of our roster,” Harris said.
The Tigers were also reluctant to add players who might eventually block those prospects. That left them trying short-term fixes like Short and, later, outfielder James Outman.
“We didn’t want to block young players,” Harris said. “We didn’t want to trade for depth players that were ultimately going to box Max out of the big leagues. So we were trying to thread that needle, and I think it probably was a mistake in the end.
“We probably should have just strengthened our depth and made sure that we could get through April and May intact.”
Harris said Detroit was particularly thin with up-the-middle defenders, back-end relievers and starting-pitching depth.
“We couldn’t really afford to lose back-end relievers,” he said. “We couldn’t really afford to lose starting depth. And we couldn’t really afford to have our pinch hitters’ performance sag in leverage spots.”
All that happened in May.
“Could we afford to have all (of that) happen at the same time? No, clearly not,” Harris said. “We went 6-22 that month, and so I feel very responsible for that.”
Too much mixing and matching
The Tigers have built much of their identity by playing the matchups, mixing and matching and asking players to be versatile.
But Harris suggested for the first time that they may have become too reliant on it.
When role players do well, like Andy Ibáñez in 2024 and Jahmai Jones in 2025, it’s a huge boost in high-leverage moments.
But when players in those roles struggle, as they did during key points in 2026, it can be devastating.
Harris sees the arrival of more players like Kevin McGonigle and Max Clark, who the Tigers believe can contribute both offensively and defensively and play nine innings every day, as a way to reduce that dependence.
“I think we’re probably going to start playing differently a little bit,” Harris said. “We’re going to be less reliant on pinch-hit appearances. We’re going to be less reliant on the mixing and matching because we have more two-way players growing through the system that can help us both defensively and offensively.”
Lagging in leverage
Based on their run differential, the Tigers had an expected record of 89-73, not 76-86.
Of course, baseball doesn’t work that way. But the gap between what actually happened and what their run differential suggests should have happened is one of the most perplexing storylines of 2026.
“When you take a look at our season, our run differential says one thing and our record says something very different,” Harris said.
“If we had played up to our run differential, we probably would have won the division again.”
“That doesn’t matter,” he added. “I can’t stand up here and just cite different metrics and tell you this is what we should have done and act like we did it. We didn’t do it.”
“So the question that I’m going to ask myself is: How do we play in a way that either meets or exceeds our run production and run prevention performance, our underlying performance?”
It’s no secret the Tigers won a lot of blowouts and lost a ton of close games. They went an astonishing 23-52 in games decided by two runs or fewer.
That’s largely because the Tigers performed better in low- and medium-leverage situations than they did when the leverage spiked.
The numbers were particularly stark among relievers.
Tigers relievers faced 370 batters in high-leverage situations and posted a jaw-dropping 9.21 ERA (5.62 FIP). Opponents posted an .855 OPS against them and hit a league-high 19 home runs in those situations. A staggering 21.8 percent of opposing fly balls landed in the seats. No other team was even close in that category.
Maybe that’s bad luck. But it’s also bad news for any team trying to contend.
“We really struggled in high leverage,” Harris said. “We’ve got to get to the bottom of that. We’ve got to figure out why that happens.”
Harris said sometimes the problem was that the game never should have reached a high-leverage situation in the first place.
“We’ve got to do a better job of staying out of those high-leverage situations,” Harris said.
That means looking beyond the final pitch of a loss.
“There were a number of games that we saw this year where we got walked off or our bullpen blew a late lead that I don’t think you can actually put on our bullpen,” Harris said.
“Some of them you can, for sure. But some of them you can’t.
“Some of them you can actually look deeper into the game and you could find the core issue, which was we didn’t create separation before, or we made a misplay in the third inning and coughed up one or two runs, or we made a baserunning mistake in the fifth inning,” Harris said.
“We let our opponent stay in the game, create this one- and two-run game, and then we ultimately lost it.”
Harris believes the changing makeup of the roster can help with that.
The Tigers are getting younger, faster and, in Harris’ view, more athletic. He expects that to mean better defense, more aggressive baserunning and more ways to create separation without simply waiting for a home run.
“We’re going to take the extra base. We’re also going to steal bases. And we’re also going to put a lot more pressure, and that’s all going to contribute to creating separation when we’re not hitting,” Harris said.
“We’re still going to hit, but we’re also going to be able to flex different muscles at different times that can help us stay out of those high-leverage situations.”
Harris said the Tigers are already conducting what he called a “pre-mortem” on the 2027 roster, trying to anticipate next year’s vulnerabilities before they arise.
“What if this happens? What are we going to do? What if this happens? What are we going to do?” Harris said.
That includes underperformance as well as injuries.
“If a guy gets out of the gate really slow, what are we going to do?” Harris said. “Those are the questions we have to ask ourselves.
“When I talk about learning lessons from the season, that’s one of the lessons that I’ve learned.”

item.title: [si.com] MLB Postseason Power Rankings: Strength and Weaknesses for Every Playoff Team
item.dc:creator: Karl Rasmussen
item.description: The postseason field is finally set. After Sunday’s results on the final day of the regular season, we officially know what 12 teams will be in contention for the 2026 World Series. The Diamondbacks, despite their late push, fell short of the playoffs, thanks to a Phillies win on Sunday against the Rays. Meanwhile, the final domino to fall in the American League went in favor of the Astros, who secured the AL West title with a victory over the Athletics on Sunday. Houston becomes the worst team
item.content:encoded:
The postseason field is finally set. After Sunday’s results on the final day of the regular season, we officially know what 12 teams will be in contention for the 2026 World Series.
The Diamondbacks, despite their late push, fell short of the playoffs, thanks to a Phillies win on Sunday against the Rays. Meanwhile, the final domino to fall in the American League went in favor of the Astros, who secured the AL West title with a victory over the Athletics on Sunday. Houston becomes the worst team to ever make the playoffs in a 162-game season, sneaking in and winning the division with just an 81–81 record.
Fans won’t have to wait long for postseason to get underway, with the Wild Card series set to begin on Tuesday. But before the action gets going, we’re going to do a final power ranking, assessing where all 12 teams sit and detailing their biggest strength and weakness.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
Biggest strength: Elite starting pitching, lineup
Biggest weakness: Bullpen
The Dodgers may be the No. 2 seed in the National League, but they’re built to win in October. It’s hard to determine what’s a greater strength between their loaded starting rotation or their star-studded lineup. There’s no weaknesses in their rotation, with All-Star caliber pitchers available to take the mound every night, even with Shohei Ohtani restricted to DH duties. There isn’t a team in MLB with more postseason experience than Los Angeles, who have won back-to-back World Series with this core. During the regular season, the Dodgers had MLB’s second-highest OPS (.762) and fourth-best ERA (3.55). If there’s any way to beat them it’s by getting after a bullpen that has been inconsistent throughout the season, though it’s still a top-10 unit. Injuries have plagued their relief pitching corps, however, with the likes of Blake Treinen, Edgardo Henriquez and Will Klein all currently on IL.
2. Milwaukee Brewers
Biggest strength: Elite pitching
Biggest weakness: Lack of power
The Brewers’ rotation, headlined by NL Cy Young favorite Jacob Misiorowski, has been one of MLB’s best, and it’s helped the team secure the league’s best regular-season record. The starting rotation owns MLB’s fifth-best ERA (3.65) and their bullpen has been equally impressive, ranking third in MLB with a 3.40 ERA. Milwaukee has scored the second-most runs in the league this season (832), as their small-ball approach has worked wonders for them. But in October, when a single swing of the bat can dramatically change a team’s fortunes and rallies are harder to come by, they might not have the power hitters capable of providing that big home run swing. The Brewers didn’t have a single 30-home run hitter this season and had just three everyday starters with a slugging percentage above .450.
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Biggest strength: Elite starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Bottom-third of the lineup
The Rays had the best record in the American League this season, largely thanks to their pitching. The starting rotation has been excellent, ranking third in MLB with a 3.51 ERA. Drew Rasmussen has quietly been one of MLB’s best arms, and Freddy Peralta has begun to rediscover his previous form after a rough go with the Mets and a shaky start on the mound in Tampa. Much like the Brewers, the Rays primarily utilize a small-ball approach offensively. The Rays hit the ninth-fewest home runs in MLB this year, and despite rostering some elite hitters such as Junior Caminero and Yandy Diaz, they haven’t received much production out of the bottom third of their lineup, which is their biggest weakness with the postseason looming.
4. Atlanta Braves
Biggest strength: Deep lineup
Biggest weakness: Plate discipline, low on-base rates
The Braves are another team with an abundance of postseason experience in the lineup. They have several players that can turn a game on its head with one swing of the bat, and had five 20-plus home run hitters during the regular season in Matt Olson, Michael Harris, Drake Baldwin, Ozzie Albies and Ronald Acuña Jr. Although the lineup is flush with talent, the group has a tendency to chase pitches out of the zone, and they don’t draw walks at a high rate. The Braves ranked 28th in MLB in on-base percentage (.309) during the regular season, often opting for an aggressive approach at the plate rather than a patient one. That could prove costly in October against some of the best pitchers in the sport, where slowing the game down and getting runners on base by any means necessary will be crucial.
5. New York Yankees
Biggest strength: Elite pitching rotation
Biggest weakness: Offense (without Aaron Judge), high strikeout rates
Yankees starting pitchers led MLB with a 3.30 ERA this season, and they’ll have one of the best rotations in the postseason with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodon set to take the mound in October. The bullpen has been a bit inconsistent, but they should be able to ride their starting rotation deep into games. The biggest weakness for the Yankees is their lineup, particularly without Aaron Judge in the mix. New York had the sixth-most strikeouts this season and were tied for 11th in MLB with a .720 OPS. With Judge out of the lineup, however, their OPS falls to a .690 mark, which would be 29th in MLB.
6. San Diego Padres
Biggest strength: Elite bullpen
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The Padres’ bullpen has been as reliable as they come this season, and the team flexes multiple elite relievers who they can reliably turn the ball over to in the later innings in Mason Miller, Yuki Matsui and Adrian Morejon, among others. San Diego has shaken off a slow start to the year and are playing at an extremely high level heading into the postseason. The offense is alive again after a dreadful first couple of months of the season, with players like Fernando Tatis Jr. and Jackson Merrill having been among MLB’s best second-half performers at the plate. The starting pitching will be the x-factor in October, however. With Casey Mize landing on the IL, their options in the rotation are even thinner. Remaining competitive within the first six innings will be crucial for the Padres, whose starting pitchers rank 21st in MLB with a 4.42 ERA this year.
7. Chicago Cubs
Biggest strength: Dominant lineup
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The Cubs have had MLB’s best offense this season, leading the league in OPS (.767), walks (674), runs scored (850) and slugging percentage (.428). They’ve been particularly elite since the All-Star break, logging a .797 OPS in their last 66 games. With Pete Crow-Armstrong playing at an MVP level and Alex Bregman having enjoyed a monster second half, the Cubs’ offense will be tough to shut down in October. Of course, they’ll need their pitching to live up to their end of the bargain, which it’s struggled to do this season. Chicago’s starting pitching has been disappointing and plagued by injuries. The starting rotation ranks 18th in MLB with a 4.27 ERA this year and have surrendered the third-most home runs (142).
8. Boston Red Sox
Biggest strength: Elite pitching
Biggest weakness: Inconsistent offense
The Red Sox’s pitching as a whole has been excellent. Boston’s bullpen owns a league-best 3.00 ERA this season, and no group of relievers in MLB has surrendered fewer home runs (55). Their starters have been great, too, ranking eighth in the league with a 3.92 ERA, and they boast a solid mix of veterans (Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez) and young, emerging starters (Payton Tolle and Jake Bennett). Offensively, however, the Red Sox have been prone to spells of inconsistency. They started the season ice cold before enjoying a scalding hot summer streak, but they’ve come crashing back down to earth in the final month of the season. The Red Sox rank dead last in MLB in OPS (.651) throughout the month of September, and they’re batting a league-worst .219 in that span.
9. Cleveland Guardians
Biggest strength: Starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Lack of power
The Guardians starting pitching has been a top-10 unit this season, ranking ninth in ERA (3.93) and fifth in strikeouts (878). Parker Messick has been superb in his first full season in MLB, and Gavin Williams has emerged as one of the league’s best strikeout pitchers. Cleveland will feel confident with those two spearheading the rotation, but they may struggle to get the run support required to take advantage of their quality starters. The Guardians rank 24th in MLB with 678 runs scored, 26th in OPS (.696) and 27th in home runs (162) this season. If they can’t come up with some big at-bats, it won’t matter how effective their pitching is in October.
10. Philadelphia Phillies
Biggest strength: Starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Defense, bullpen
The Phillies have one of the best starting rotations in MLB, but they’ve been plagued by some underperforming position players and a lackluster bullpen. There’s arguably no better trio of starters in MLB than Cristopher Sánchez, Zack Wheeler and Jesús Luzardo. The team’s starting rotation ranks seventh in the league with a 3.80 ERA, but their bullpen ranks 21st in ERA (4.43). Defensively, the Phillies have been atrocious, too. Only the Athletics have fewer defensive runs saved than the Phillies’ -43, according to the Fielding Bible, and the infield has been a serious concern, with Trea Turner, Bryce Harper and Alec Bohm all ranking among the bottom 26 defensive players (of 270 qualified players) in MLB in terms of outs above average, per Statcast. Defensive shortcomings and mishaps could prove highly costly in October, and that’s an area that’s plagued Philadelphia all season.
11. Chicago White Sox
Biggest strength: Power hitting
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The White Sox have a potent lineup and are the only team in MLB that have three players who hit 30 or more home runs in Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami and Colson Montgomery. Chicago hit the fifth-most home runs this season (211) and scored the fifth-most runs (776). While the offense is among the league’s best in terms of power, the White Sox starting pitching is a serious concern. The starting rotation posted a season ERA of 4.60 (fourth-worst in MLB), a 1.34 WHIP (sixth-worst in MLB) and recorded the third-fewest strikeouts of any starting rotation in the league. Chicago’s starters also threw the fewest innings in MLB this season, often struggling to get deep into games before the baton was passed to the bullpen. If the starting rotation can’t keep runs off the board, it might not matter how explosive their lineup can be.
12. Houston Astros
Biggest strength: Power hitting
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
Yordan Alvarez is likely to win the AL MVP, and he’s the type of hitter teams will not be eager to pitch to in October. No team in MLB hit more home runs than the Astros, who hit 226. In addition to Alvarez’s 42, Houston had four other players with 20-plus homers, including Christian Walker (29), Isaac Paredes (25), Jeremy Peña (22) and Cam Smith (21). They don’t have much to worry about offensively, but their lineup will need to produce in order to ease the burden on their starting rotation, which has largely struggled this year. Hunter Brown remains a reliable ace, but beyond him there’s a lack of experience and talent within the rotation. Astros starters ranked 27th in MLB with a 4.81 ERA and 1.40 WHIP, both of which were the worst among all teams that qualified for the postseason, and they walked the most batters in MLB this season. If the lineup can’t make up for the rotation’s shortcomings, it could be a short postseason stint for Houston this year.
Karl Rasmussen is a staff writer for Sports Illustrated. A University of Oregon alum who joined SI in February 2023, his work has appeared on 12up and ClutchPoints. Rasmussen is a loyal Tottenham, Jets, Yankees and Ducks fan.
Follow Karlras920

item.title: [si.com] The Potentially Fatal Flaw For Each MLB Playoff Team
item.dc:creator: Ryan Phillips
item.description: The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early. With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team. Brewers: Lack of Power The Brewers were baseball’s best team
item.content:encoded:
The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early.
With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team.
Brewers: Lack of Power
The Brewers were baseball’s best team all season but that doesn’t mean they’re perfect. Milwaukee has a great rotation fronted by baseball’s new ace Jacob Misiorowski, and a good bullpen, but the lineup relies heavily on getting hits up and down the lineup. The Brewers play the 2026 version of small ball, and don’t have a ton of power. That can kill teams in October, when runs come at a premium.
Milwaukee finished the season tied for 28th in home runs (154) and 25th in isolated power (.144). The Brewers were tied for 10th in slugging (.403) and were third in wRC+ (107), but the lack of top-line power could be their downfall. Against elite pitching in the postseason, it’s much more difficult to string together hits and build big innings. Being able to get runs on balls that leave the yard is huge. Each of the last six World Series champions ranked inside the top five in regular season home runs.
Maybe Milwaukee bucks that trend, but if they don’t win the World Series, a lack of power may be the reason.
Dodgers: Health
The Dodgers have won two straight titles and at full strength, they’d be the overwhelming favorite to take home a third in a row. But L.A. has dealt with major injuries all season and the team looks more vulnerable than it has in a long time as we enter the postseason.
Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow combined to make only 22 starts this season. Both are back now, but neither has been particularly reliable—Snell left his penultimate start on Sept. 16 with a groin injury before returning to pitch four innings on Saturday. Tarik Skubal had elbow surgery earlier this year with the Tigers and hasn’t been quite as dominant as usual when it comes to limiting baserunners. Shohei Ohtani has been sidelined by knee and biceps injuries, and won’t be pitching in October. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernandez are showing signs of decline and have played a ton of baseball over the last three years.
L.A. is still loaded, but a few injuries to a roster that’s had its fair share of medical issues could make things dicey.
Rays: Trouble Against Lefties
It’s hard to find too many flaws here. The Rays are an incredibly balanced squad that was the best in the AL pretty much all season. One of the only red flags here is the team’s performance against lefties, and they’re likely to run into a few in the playoffs.
Against lefties as a team, Tampa Bay ranked 27th in slugging (.364), 26th in wRC+ (90) and 25th in OPS (.679). Luckily for the Rays, their best offensive players hammered lefties. Junior Caminero slashed .287/.426/.490 with eight home runs and a 152 wRC+. Unfortunately, the 23-year-old and Yandy Diaz are the team’s only players who appeared in 100-plus games and topped .700 in OPS against lefties.
That’s a weakness opponents will try to exploit in October. The Rays don’t have many holes, but good left-handed pitching could be the kryptonite that slows one of baseball’s most complete teams.
Braves: A Hole at Shortstop
The Braves have plenty of star power in the lineup and Chris Sale at the top of their rotation but they have a huge flaw at the heart of their team. Atlanta’s shortstops were among the worst offensively during the 2026 season. Ha-seong Kim is is the starter, but he had a .359 OPS with zero home runs in 147 plate appearances this season so I’m not sure that is the answer. The other option is Mauricio Dubón, who had a .719 OPS in 153 games, but that won’t work against southpaws since it means lefty Mike Yastrzemski must play left field.
Collectively, Braves shortstops slashed .241/.295/.349 during the regular season and ranked 27th with a wRC+ of 78. They also ranked 23rd in fWAR (1.6) and bWAR (-0.4). They simply haven’t gotten enough out of the position and need to find some offensive production there.
Atlanta went wire-to-wire to win the NL East and did so while not getting much from a premium position. Against elite pitching in the postseason, they’ll need production out of everyone in the lineup at some point. Carrying an empty spot will likely prove to be more damaging than it already has been.
Yankees: An Aaron Judge-Sized Hole in the Lineup
The Yankees may have baseball’s best postseason rotation and found enough offense to hold onto the AL’s top wild-card spot. But to win a World Series, they need their best player healthy and hammering baseballs. They may not have it.
Aaron Judge is trying to return for the wild-card series from a strained calf muscle, but it would be unwise to rush him back into action. Yes, New York needs his bat in the lineup, but it also needs to ensure he is available for the entire postseason, not just the first series. Ben Rice (149), Cody Bellinger (115) and Paul Goldschmidt (111) are the only Yankees with more than 300 plate appearances and a wRC+ over 100. That’s a scary lack of production from the lineup.
They need Judge’s bat back at full health as soon as possible simply because the team relies on him so much to produce.
Padres: Who Starts After Michael King?
The Padres have baseball’s best bullpen and an offense that has been clicking on all cylinders in the second half. What they don’t have is a deep rotation after injuries have decimated it.
Michael King is the team’s ace and should be reliable in that spot, but after him things get dicey. Nick Pivetta missed most of the season due to a flexor strain in his pitching elbow that cost him nearly five months. He’s back and has thrown well, but he’s only made eight starts this year. After that, it’ll be some combination of Robbie Ray and Walker Buehler. Both have been up and down this season and neither feels like a rock-solid option.
If San Diego can get decent starts and shorten games by getting the bullpen in early, things could be fine. But if the team’s starters struggle it could mean an early exit.
Cubs: A Battered Starting Rotation
The Cubs have one of baseball’s best offenses and its best all-around player in Pete Crow-Armstrong, but their pitching staff remains a patchwork mess. The team’s starting rotation has endured season-ending injuries to Cade Horton and Ben Brown, Justin Steele still hasn’t returned after elbow surgery in 2025, Matthew Boyd missed time thanks to knee surgery and a shoulder issue, and Kevin Gausman is now dealing with a shoulder injury.
Chicago will open the postseason with Boyd on the mound and should follow with Clay Holmes in Game 2, then Shota Imanaga and, if he’s healthy enough, Gausman. How bad has it been for the Cubs? Among starters, only Imanaga generated 2.0 bWAR this year. That’s a dangerous weakness to carry into the postseason when pitching becomes even more important.
Could the Cubs manage to overcome a rotation that has been battered all season? It’s possible, but that would take a herculean effort from the team’s top-ranked offense.
Phillies: Trea Turner’s Disappearing Production
Trea Turner was a key piece of the Phillies’ success in 2025, as he slashed .302/.354/.450 with 15 home runs, 36 stolen bases and a 123 wRC+ in 141 games. The team is probably wondering where that guy went.
In 157 games this year, Turner slashed .242/.297/.378 with 19 home runs, 21 stolen bases and a wRC+ of 83. His strikeout rate jumped from 16.7% to 21.0%, his xBA dropped from .270 to .242 and his xwOBA of .293 ranked in the 14th percentile. That would be manageable if Turner provided value defensively, but his outs above average dropped from 17 in 2025 to -8 this season. That’s a precipitous, ominous drop for a shortstop who’s in his age-33 season, has always depended on his athleticism and still has seven more years on his contract. Philadelphia has underachieved as a whole in 2026, and Turner is the poster child.
While he was a disappointment in the regular season, Turner has a ton of playoff experience and won a title with the Nationals in 2019. Maybe he’ll turn it around when the lights are the brightest. But his postseason track record doesn’t offer much optimism. He has a career playoff OPS of .681.
Red Sox: A Top-Heavy Offense
Boston’s comeback story this season was remarkable after Alex Cora was fired following a 10–17 start. While they were one of MLB’s best teams over the final two-thirds of the season, the offense never really clicked one through nine. As a team, the Red Sox finished 17th in wRC+ (99) and 19th in OPS (.717). And it seemed all season a few guys would come through, while the rest of the lineup struggled.
Among the team’s hitters who played at least 100 games, only Willson Contreras (151), Wilyer Abreu (112) and Ceddanne Rafaela (109) topped 100 in wRC+ to grade out as above-average hitters. The drop-off from Contreras to the rest of the roster is pretty alarming in itself, though Mickey Gasper (130), Masataka Yoshida (108) and Roman Anthony (106) all performed well in fewer than 300 plate appearances. Key pieces like Caleb Durbin (100) and especially Jarren Duran (69) had off years, while catcher Adley Rutschman slashed .222/.278/.410 with a wRC+ of 88 after arriving at the trade deadline.
Boston will have to overcome those issues throughout the lineup, particularly against the kind of pitching ahead in the postseason. The lack of offensive balance could be the team’s downfall.
Guardians: A Lineup Short of Firepower
The Guardians are in an enviable position, as they barely made the playoffs but wound up with the AL’s No. 2 seed. While they are set up for success thanks to the bracket and have an excellent pitching staff, their lineup has been anemic.
Cleveland finished the regular season ranked 27th in home runs (162) and slugging (.380), 26th in OPS (.696), 24th in runs scored (678) and 21st in wRC+ (97). Meanwhile, star third baseman José Ramírez wrapped up the worst full season of his career, slashing .235/.320/.368 with 12 home runs and a wRC+ of 92. The question is simple: Where do the runs come from? Rookie Chase DeLauter was the team’s most productive hitter after slashing .287/.363/.456 with 16 home runs and a 131 wRC+, but he doesn't have much help. Steven Kwan was second on the team in wRC+ (114), but only slugged .349, while Travis Bazzana (110) and Angel Martinez (108) were both only modestly above average by wRC+. The rest of the lineup struggled to generate offense.
After a tough battle down the stretch, the Guardians wound up with a favorable path in the postseason. But getting to the World Series will likely require unearthing some unsung heroes on offense.
White Sox: October Inexperience
The White Sox surprised everyone with their run to a postseason berth after three consecutive 100-loss seasons. The roster has been properly overhauled, with only 19.8% of the team’s plate appearances coming from players on the 121-loss team in 2024. The problem is, most of the team’s new players have little to no postseason experience.
Braden Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Sam Antonacci are rookies, while Colson Montgomery, Kyle Teel, Chase Meidroth and Grant Taylor are second-year players. Sean Burke debuted in 2024, but has never pitched in the postseason, and All-Star Miguel Vargas has likewise never appeared in the postseason despite coming up with the Dodgers. Maybe there’s something to be said for youthful exuberance, but there’s also the possibility that fatigue becomes a factor for players who haven’t been through a playoff chase before. Colson Montgomery posted a wRC+ of 54 after August 1, while Murakami slashed .156/.299/.375 in that stretch.
Chicago is built for success long-term, but its lack of postseason experience could be a significant obstacle in October.
Astros: A Thin Starting Rotation
The Astros finished 81–81 to win the weak AL West and notch a playoff spot. Given their record, it’s not surprising they have a ton of issues across the roster. The most glaring is their starting rotation, which is in rough shape.
Beyond Hunter Brown, Houston simply doesn’t have the kind of high-end starting pitching that wins in October. And even Brown enters the playoffs with some uncertainty, having thrown only 107 ⅓ innings this season after missing a chunk of the campaign with a shoulder injury. Peter Lambert has become the team’s No. 2 starter, but he went 8–10 with a 3.82 ERA and doesn’t possess premium stuff. Hayden Wesneski finished the season strong, but made only 11 starts all year, while Cristian Javier and Mike Burrows are both on the IL.
The rotation is so thin that the Astros are poised to open Game 1 of the wild-card series with a bullpen game to give Brown, Lambert and Wesneski rest. It’s hardly an ideal situation and there aren’t many options available for manager Joe Espada.
Ryan Phillips is a senior writer on the Breaking and Trending News team at Sports Illustrated. He has worked in digital media since 2009, spending eight years at The Big Lead before joining SI in 2024. Phillips also co-hosts The Assembly Call Podcast about Indiana Hoosiers basketball and previously worked at Bleacher Report. He is a proud San Diego native and a graduate of Indiana University’s journalism program.

item.dc:creator: Michael DeRosa
item.description: On Tuesday, the Philadelphia Phillies kick off their NL Wild Card series against the Atlanta Braves. The Phillies will be looking to start their series against the Braves on the right foot by picking up a victory. Now, as the Phillies prepare for Game 1 against the Braves, they have announced a notable lineup decision with superstar slugger Kyle Schwarber. item.content:encoded:
On Tuesday, the Philadelphia Phillies kick off their NL Wild Card series against the Atlanta Braves.
The Phillies will be looking to start their series against the Braves on the right foot by picking up a victory.
Now, as the Phillies prepare for Game 1 against the Braves, they have announced a notable lineup decision with superstar slugger Kyle Schwarber.
Kyle Schwarber Batting Second for Phillies for Game 1 vs Braves
The Phillies have revealed their batting order for their Game 1 matchup against the Braves. Schwarber will not be in his usual leadoff spot, as he will be batting second for Philadelphia.
Schwarber was mainly the Phillies’ leadoff hitter this campaign but did bat second in each of Philadelphia’s final two regular season games. Now, he will be batting second for Philadelphia again in Game 1 against Atlanta.
Here is Philadelphia’s full batting order, as reported by Underdog MLB: T. Turner SS K. Schwarber DH B. Harper RF A. Bohm 1B D. Hill CF B. De La Cruz LF B. Stott 2B E. Sosa 3B J. Realmuto C
Phillies 9/29
T. Turner SS
K. Schwarber DH
B. Harper RF
A. Bohm 1B
D. Hill CF
B. De La Cruz LF
B. Stott 2B
E. Sosa 3B
J. Realmuto C
J. Luzardo SP
— Underdog MLB (@UnderdogMLB) September 29, 2026
Looking at Schwarber
Schwarber had another strong regular season for Philadelphia in 2026. In 156 games with the Phillies this campaign, the 12-year MLB veteran posted 45 home runs, 97 RBI, and a .232 batting average. This is after he had 56 home runs, 132 RBI, and a .240 batting average in 156 games for Philadelphia in 2025.
Schwarber will now be looking to have a good postseason. If the Phillies hope to get by the Braves, they will need him on his A-game.

Atlanta opens a best-of-three National League Wild Card Series against the Philadelphia Phillies at Truist Park on Tuesday afternoon. Now Atlanta will try to carry it into a series against the division rival that eliminate
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA - The Braves are back in the postseason, and their first opponent is a familiar one. Atlanta opens a best-of-three National League Wild Card Series against the Philadelphia Phillies at Truist Park on Tuesday afternoon.
PREVIOUS STORY: Braves, Phillies meet again as playoffs return to Truist Park
"Let it fly" is the Braves’ postseason message, drawn from a spring training speech by manager Walt Weiss. Now Atlanta will try to carry it into a series against the division rival that eliminated the Braves from the playoffs in both 2022 and 2023.
Sale gets the Game 1 start
Chris Sale will start Tuesday’s opener. He told FOX 5 Atlanta that pitching a postseason game at home for the Braves means a great deal to him.
First baseman Matt Olson said the late-season meetings with Philadelphia have given the teams added familiarity heading into the series. The Braves went 4-10 against the Phillies in their previous postseason meetings, but Sale had success against them this regular season: Atlanta won all four of his starts against Philadelphia, according to MLB.
Game 2 is scheduled for Wednesday. A deciding Game 3 would be played Thursday if needed.
Pregame party at The Battery
Crews were preparing the field and stands Tuesday morning as fans got ready to return to Truist Park for playoff baseball.
A Braves block party is scheduled to start at 11 a.m. at The Battery Atlanta, with a BMX stunt show among the planned entertainment.
Truist Park gates open at noon, two hours before first pitch. Watch parties are also planned at The Battery during the Braves’ postseason run, including when the team plays on the road.
Fans looking for something new inside the ballpark can try the "Grand Slam Tail," a lobster tail stuffed with crab and shrimp, wrapped in wonton skin and fried.
And just in case baseball fans need a written excuse to get out of work or school to catch the game, the Braves kindly posted a form on social media.

item.content:encoded:
JustPredictions
Justice editors predict the upcoming year of sports.
Ben Khayat ’28: Only one Big Ten team will make the College Football Playoffs. The sample size is small, but the Big Ten has been downright shameful to start the 2026 season. The obvious examples are the Michigan Wolverines coming back from the dead to prevent a home loss to the Western Michigan Broncos, and the Rutgers Scarlet Knights succumbing to the UMass Minutemen, a team that didn’t win a single game last season. The rest of the conference hasn’t been much better. The Oregon Ducks came into the season ranked #2 in the country, but came up limping in their one-score win over the Boise State Broncos before getting dispatched by Oklahoma State on Saturday. The Ohio State Buckeyes led 23-3 against the Texas Longhorns, only to allow 21 unanswered points and choke what would have been the first statement win the conference has had this season. Come January, I can’t imagine many of these “top” teams will have impressed anybody enough to get an at-large bid over some other power conference opponents.
Luca D. Jordan ’28: The Chicago Bears will make the Superbowl this season. After having an amazing breakout season under head coach Ben Johnson and making their first playoff appearance since 2020, the Chicago Bears have shown explosive growth with a new offensive direction. Defined by their comeback wins, the Bears almost clinched the semi-finals last season, but quarterback Caleb Williams threw a bad pass that led to an interception against the Los Angeles Rams. Despite an unfortunate play that ended his season early, Williams has shown flashes of an all time great quarterback. When it comes down to the last few seconds, Williams is known to perform herculean throws to save the game. Although their offseason wasn’t particularly exciting, expect a surprising surge in performance across the board from the entire roster. Previous champs Seattle Seahawks are dead in the water without Sam Darnold and the Rams have added some big names to their roster, but it’s just stars over substance. The Bears have a few decades of an underdog legacy behind them, and that’s too much destiny to ignore.
Bryan Wolfe ’27: The New York Knicks are running it back! I have faith. Even though the Philadelphia 76ers have the starting five of doom and despair, I believe in the king of New York Jalen Brunson to lead us back to the promised land.
Chava Thiell ’29: Alexander Zverev will finish the 2026 ATP season with an ATP finals win and the World #1 ranking. As unfortunate as it may be for diehard Sincaraz fans, Jannik Sinner isn’t healthy and Carlos Alcaraz is still adjusting to his return to tennis after a four-month hiatus. After Zverev clinched two Slams this year, his momentum cannot seem to be stopped. Conversely, I think Aryba Sabalenka will walk away with the WTA Finals trophy, inspired by a heartbreaking US Open final loss to rival Elena Rybakina and a mission to come away from the season with a big tournament win.
Eli Sandalow ’28: The New England Patriots will go 4-13. Drake Maye looks like he regressed, AJ Brown is prone to long-term injuries and Rhamondre Stevenson is one of the most overrated running backs in the NFL right now.
Alyssa Wu ‘29: The Dodgers won’t three-peat this year.The Dodgers have a stacked lineup, with Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman and Mookie Betts, plus a star-studded starting rotation of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. Along with their veterans, new acquisitions this year include stars like Tarik Skubal, a two-time American League Cy Young winner. Despite this, the Dodgers have not dominated through the season as many expected. They went 13-14 in August, though they have found their footing again in September. Injuries raise more concerns; Ohtani only returned to the lineup on September 23 after a stint on the injured list and is not expected to pitch for the remainder of the season. Reliever Blake Treinen, who has helped bring three championships to the Dodgers in his six seasons, suffered a season-ending injury on September 26. With Kyle Tucker and Andy Pages being the only starting position players under the age of 30, the question is whether these Dodger veterans will be healthy and as productive as they used to be during the postseason. The MLB Playoff bracket itself does not always reward the ‘best’ team. The Dodgers in 2022 are one of the clearest examples of this. In 2022, they went 111-51 and won 14 of 19 regular-season games against the Padres. However, after winning Game 1 of the NLDS, they lost three straight to the San Diego Padres, ending their season. The postseason can bring plenty of surprises, and a team’s regular season does not always predict its success in the playoffs. The Dodgers had to come back from a 3-2 deficit to win last year’s World Series, and this year’s team seems to be much more vulnerable. The Dodgers are sure to make it far in the playoffs, but another championship is far from guaranteed.

Good morning! Playoff baseball begins today with the Philadelphia Phillies vs. the Atlanta Braves in NL Wild Card Game 1 and Boston Red Sox vs. New York Yankees in AL Wild Card Game 1.
Which AL and NL team(s) are you rooting for in this year’s MLB Postseason?
In Mariners news…
- Longtime Bench Coach Manny Acta, Infield Coach Perry Hill, Hitting Coach Kevin Seitzer, and First Base Coach Eric Young Jr. will not return for the 2027 season as part of an organizational culture reset.
- The Mariners are reportedly seeking an experienced manager to replace Dan Wilson and have discussed Arizona Diamondbacks manager Torey Lovullo as a potential candidate.
- Congrats to Kade Anderson’s on winning Baseball America’s 2026 Minor League Pitcher of the Year!
Around the league…
- The New York Yankees are not ruling slugger Aaron Judge out of the team’s Wild Card series as he pushes to return from a strained right calf muscle.
- The Chicago Cubs’ investment in innovative bat technology is part of a growing trend within the league. ($)
- Philadelphia Phillies second baseman Luis Arraez will miss the NL Wild Card Series with a sprained left ankle.
- The Toronto Blue Jays are expected to pursue outfielder Seiya Suzuki when he hits free agency.
- Baltimore Orioles RHP Kyle Bradish is set to undergo hernia surgery after dealing with a hernia during his final three starts of the season.
- Mike Petriello at MLB.com highlights both the offensive and defensive success of Pete Crow-Armstrong’s historic 2026 season.

item.title: [roundtable.io] Orioles' Pete Alonso Makes History In First Season Away From New York
item.dc:creator: Chris Traczek
item.description: Opinions of the disastrous 2026 New York Mets season will continue to go from bad to worse as erstwhile franchise icon Pete Alonso sets single-season MLB RBI record in first season with Baltimore Orioles. It's bad enough that almost all of their offseason moves prior to the 2026 season failed because of either subpar player performance or injuries, but their most high-profile decision - choosing not to offer free-agent first baseman Pete Alonso a contract - just went from bad to worse. That's be
item.content:encoded:
Opinions of the disastrous 2026 New York Mets season will continue to go from bad to worse as erstwhile franchise icon Pete Alonso sets single-season MLB RBI record in first season with Baltimore Orioles.
It's bad enough that almost all of their offseason moves prior to the 2026 season failed because of either subpar player performance or injuries, but their most high-profile decision - choosing not to offer free-agent first baseman Pete Alonso a contract - just went from bad to worse.
That's because the beloved "Polar Bear" concluded the first season of his five-year, $155-million contract with the Baltimore Orioles by leading the American League with 113 RBIs. Coupled with the 131 RBIs he had for the Mets in 2022, which led the National League, Alonso is now the first player in MLB history to lead each league in RBIs in a season. For context, RBIs became an official stat in 1920 and for 106 years no one had done what Alonso just did.
Additionally, Alonso also led the AL with 43 home runs, which gave him a bookend for the NL-best 53 homers he hit while winning NL Rookie of the Year for the Mets in 2019. It also made him the sixth player to win an HR title in both leagues, joining Shohei Ohtani, Mark McGwire, Fred McGriff, Sam Crawford and Buck Freeman.
“He could very well be a Hall of Famer when it’s all said and done,” said left-handed reliever Trevor Rogers. “The fact that I played with him and saw how he went about his business every day, it’s special.”
Added shortstop Gunnar Henderson: “His year has been unbelievable. You just laugh every time he hits a homer now. It’s so cool to watch. It’s so fun to be a part of and to be on the team with him. He’s been just awesome to have around, and [I'm] really looking forward to playing with him for many years.”
When the Mets chose not to re-sign Alonso after he opted out of his pact following the 2025 season, the reasoning was that as Alonso moved into his 30s his fielding at first base, which had never been stellar, would continue to decline. A case could be made for that, but that case went out the window when New York subsequently signed Jorge Polanco, who was two years older than Alonso and had played a grand total of one game at first in his career, to replace Alonso.
That decision came crashing down on the Mets in mid-September when Alonso and Baltimore visited Citi Field for three games. With the adoring Mets fans cheering his every move, Alonso chose the series to hit his 300th career homer, which even got a standing ovation from New York owner Steve Cohen.
In all, Alonso hit two HRs as the Orioles swept the series, with that home run total matching what Polanco produced in 37 injury-plagued games for the Mets this season.
For his part, Alonso has moved on, professing frustration that the Orioles were unable to advance to the playoffs this season, but vowing to do all he could to make the postseason a reality for his new team in 2027.
“I just want to leave it all out there,” Alonso said, according to the MLB.com report. “I really love playing the game, and for me, I just want to be all I can be and do whatever I can every single night to win the game, you know? I really take pride in wanting to win and giving it all I have.”

item.title: [arkansasonline.com] This could be MLB’s last postseason for a while with a lockout looming, players vowing to fight cap | Arkansas Democrat Gazette
item.dc:creator: RONALD BLUM AP Baseball Writer

That's why they pay us a lot." Baseball's five-year labor contract expires Dec. 1 and manageme
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK -- Days before the start of what could be Major League Baseball's last postseason for a while, Carlos Rodon was prepared for a long lockout if owners keep their salary cap proposal on the bargaining table.
"We won't play. I'm going to be frank with you," the New York Yankees pitcher said. "I'm not worried about it. They should be worried about it. There's a lot of money on us playing baseball. That's why they pay us a lot."
Baseball's five-year labor contract expires Dec. 1 and management is expected to impose a lockout that would stop trades and free-agent signings, then potentially threaten the start of spring training workouts on Feb. 9 and opening day on March 24.
When management last proposed a cap, it sparked a 7 1/2-month strike in 1994 and '95 that led to the first cancellation of the World Series in 90 years. MLB says a cap is needed to alleviate economic disparity, highlighting that no low-revenue team has won the title since the 2015 Kansas City Royals.
"The salary cap and floor proposal levels the playing field, allowing us greater flexibility to address longstanding player priorities while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50/50," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said.
Owners would also gain more financial certainty with a cap, which likely would spark an increase in franchise values.
Players point out teams with low payrolls, Milwaukee and Tampa Bay, had the best regular-season records in their leagues this season.
"Despite MLB claiming they need a salary cap because small-market teams supposedly have no hope, we see Milwaukee with the best record in baseball for the second straight year and Tampa with the best record in the AL," union head Bruce Meyer said. "Milwaukee, of course, is 30th out of 30 in our market-size rankings."
While this would be MLB's 10th work stoppage, the sport hasn't lost any regular-season games since the 1994-95 strike. Baseball players say they will never accept a cap similar to those that have been in the NFL since 1994, the NBA since 1984-85 and the NHL since 2005-06. Nine of the 10 biggest sports contracts by total value in North America belong to MLB players.
"For me the biggest thing is doing right for the generations forward because the generations before me, for the decades before, they've fought for our rights today," Baltimore first baseman Pete Alonso said. "That's a sacrifice that not just myself but other men around the league are willing to fight for and put up with."
MLB's proposal would cap team spending next year at $245.3 million, using figures for luxury tax payrolls that include an estimated $23 million for benefits and the pre-arbitration bonus pool. It also would establish a payroll floor of $171.2 million for 2027 but teams could drop as low as $154.1 million and make up the difference over the following two years. The New York Mets' opening day payroll in 2026 was more than $352 million.
Contracts would be limited by service time: $500 million and 12 years for those yet to make major league debuts down to $265 million and six years for free-agent-eligible players. It would outlaw megadeals like outfielder Juan Soto's record 15-year, $765 million contract with the Mets.
While MLB proposed to split revenues 50-50, the union says that would lead to a massive decrease in money to players because of the way revenues and expenses are defined and the player portion is calculated. In addition, an escrow provision to set salaries aside in case the players' defined revenue share is above 50% means money in guaranteed contracts could be forfeited.
MLB as part of a cap system would agree to drop service time for free agent eligibility for some players from six years of service to five and to eliminate qualifying offers, but the union maintains that would shift money among players under a cap rather than increase spending.
Alonso would lose $165,775 next year for each regular-season day missed and Rodon would forfeit $144,385.
Los Angeles Dodgers star Shohei Ohtani would give up $374,331 daily and Soto $227,273.
At the other end of the salary scale, players making MLB's proposed $900,000 minimum would lose $4,813 daily. Among the 1,366 players on rosters as of Monday, 549 (40%) started 2026 with less than one year of service time and 893 (65%) had less than three years. Players aren't eligible for salary arbitration until they've completed three seasons, with some exceptions.
Some players are protected financially because of signing bonuses that will continue to be paid during a work stoppage: Toronto first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr. is due $14 million on June 30 as part of his $325 million contract, though he would give up $74,866 daily in salary.
Tony Clark, the former All-Star first baseman who had headed the union since 2013, was forced out in February and replaced by Meyer, his deputy and chief negotiator in 2021-22.
Baltimore pitcher Chris Bassitt, a member of the union's eight-man executive subcommittee, said there had been a transformation this year in communications within the players' association. The subcommittee and the 30 team player representatives form the executive council that makes union decisions.
"Our last CBA from a player's side was not internally handled great. I think the structure was very archaic, so to speak, like an old-school approach," he said. "We have made it our mission to kind of get all 30 clubs -- 30 reps that genuinely care. And then not just 30 reps that genuinely care, but 30 reps that are making sure all their players are very informed."
When players and MLB agreed to a deal on March 10, 2022, that ended the lockout, the executive subcommittee voted 8-0 against accepting it, but the team player representatives favored the agreement by 26-4.
The vast majority of the 1,200 players on 40-man rosters when the lockout starts will not have salary arbitration or free agency rights and will have 2027 salaries under $1 million.
"Their voices matter, what they're feeling, what they're thinking," Bassitt said. "When I came in the league it was -- I'm going to say it plainly -- but it was like: 'Rookie shut up and sit in the corner and the veterans are going to take care of this.' I don't think that's a possible avenue to go down anymore. I think the league's too young, first and foremost. Second, I think the only way to have veteran guys that are informed and understand the process is to start the education process from day one."

Field Level Media

29 Sep 2026, 06:49 GMT+10

(Photo credit: David Frerker)
The Chicago Cubs eliminated the San Diego Padres from the postseason a year ago and then scored 55 runs while going 5-1 against them this season.
But nobody is expecting that type of one-sided matchup to continue as the Padres are hotter than lava entering Tuesday night's National League wild-card series opener against visiting Chicago.
The Padres (91-71) are a sizzling 41-18 since July 24, transforming a bumbling campaign into a third straight postseason berth, a first in franchise history.
In the final days of the season, San Diego overtook the Cubs (89-73) to secure the No. 4 seed, granting the Padres home-field advantage in the best-of-three series. Chicago, the No. 5 seed, hosted at Wrigley Field last season and beat the Padres in three games in the wild-card round.
Playing the series at pitcher-friendly Petco Park could lessen the Cubs' offensive advantage. Chicago led the majors with 850 runs this season, while the Padres scored 722.
The Cubs feature leading NL MVP candidate Pete Crow-Armstrong, who recorded a 40-40 season by tying for the major league lead with 45 homers and adding 41 steals. He also led the majors with 84 extra-base hits and 119 runs.
Crow-Armstrong batted .364 (8-for-22) with four homers and 10 RBIs against San Diego this season.
'I'm looking forward to playing a really good ballclub and getting another crack at them and starting this playoffs off on a high note,' Crow-Armstrong said Monday.
San Diego's Manny Machado batted a career-low .217 but smacked 30 homers, marking the eighth time in his career he has hit at least that many.
More important to the Padres is Fernando Tatis Jr., who didn't hit his first homer until May 30 and had just five at the All-Star break. He hit 20 blasts after the break and was a major catalyst for the team's torrid 59-game finish.
'It's a baseball game. We have to get 27 outs and hopefully be the last team standing,' Machado said.
Right-hander Michael King (12-10, 3.21 ERA) will start for the Padres against Cubs left-hander Matthew Boyd (10-5, 3.91).
King has made two career postseason starts, both in 2024 for the Padres. The most memorable one came in Game 1 of the wild-card series against the Atlanta Braves when he tossed seven shutout innings and struck out 12.
King gave up one hit and struck out three in one inning of relief against the Cubs in the 2025 postseason series, his lone appearance against them with the Padres. He also twice faced Chicago in relief when he was with the New York Yankees.
'Very professional lineup,' King said of the Cubs. 'They were first in runs this year and it shows. I keep saying that when the pitcher executes, we have the upper hand so I have to make sure I am executing throughout and putting up as many zeroes as I can.'
Chicago's Alex Bregman is 7-for-8 with two doubles against King.
Bregman surged over the final two months, delivering 17 homers and 46 RBIs to get his season outputs to 28 and 93, respectively.
Bregman is playing with multiple fractures in his left cheek after getting hit by a foul ball off the bat of teammate Michael Busch during a game on Sept. 20.
Boyd, 35, is 0-1 with a 1.66 ERA in seven playoff appearances (six starts). He was 0-1 with a 2.79 ERA in three starts for Chicago last postseason and gave up one run and four hits over 4 1/3 innings when the Cubs beat the Padres in Game 1 of last year's wild-card series.
'The Padres are one of the hottest teams in baseball the past few weeks,' Boyd said. 'That's not surprising. We've seen them firsthand -- this year, last year. I always firmly believe that it's more about what's in this clubhouse and less about what's on the other side. Take care of your business.'
Boyd is 2-1 with a 4.43 ERA in four regular-season outings against San Diego. Machado is 9-for-20 (.450) with a homer and four doubles against Boyd.
The winner of this series faces the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Division Series.
--Field Level Media

item.title: [sfexaminer.com] No matter who wins, MLB will push salary cap
item.dc:creator: Ken Rosenthal; The Athletic

item.content:encoded:
(Commentary)
Here's the thing about all the agita related to the Los Angeles Dodgers, MLB's competitive balance and the 2026 postseason: No outcome this October will change the calculus for the team owners.
Even if the small-market Milwaukee Brewers, Tampa Bay Rays or Cleveland Guardians win the World Series, the league will continue its push for a salary cap, contending the sport lacks sufficient parity and is effectively broken.
Not that long ago, the league was making precisely the opposite argument. Its public-relations department, in news releases before the 2021 and 2022 seasons, described competitive balance as a hallmark of MLB.
Let's be clear: Revenue disparity between large- and small-market clubs is a legitimate concern. The league and players union need to adopt significant measures to make the playing field more level. But the league's argument for greater competitive balance, if not a red herring, is at least an argument of convenience. And not a particularly strong one, if you watched the regular season.
The Brewers finished with the best record in the National League. The Rays produced the best record in the American League. And the Guardians became the third small-market team to earn one of four first-round byes. Perhaps the Guardians were undeserving, considering their record was only the 11th best in the majors. But by finishing with the second-best mark among AL division winners, they clinched the bye under the postseason format the league and union created.
So is the sport really that far gone?
The league's own news release in 2022 noted that MLB produced 15 different World Series champions in the prior 21 seasons. The Texas Rangers in 2023 made it 16. And before the 2024 World Series, MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred told The Athletic, "Our record on competitive balance is darn good."
Just two years later, to hear Manfred & Co. tell it, the sport is having an existential crisis. All because the league's highest-revenue team, the Dodgers, won back-to-back World Series. All because the team owners want to build their case for a cap.
The league cites a need for greater competitive balance as justification to drastically overhaul the game's economic system. And it is trumpeting a new set of facts -- specifically, the absence of a small-market champion since the 2015 Kansas City Royals -- to make its case.
There is no denying that in that time, large-market teams have accounted for 90% of World Series winners, 85% of World Series participants and 77.5% of league championship series participants. And sure, the same pattern might continue this year.
Never mind that the Dodgers performed below expectations in the regular season for the second consecutive year. According to FanGraphs, they still stand the best chance of winning the World Series -- 36.7%, with the Brewers next at 11.6%. As if on cue, and in some cases by design, the Dodgers' best players are getting healthy and rounding into form.
If Los Angeles becomes the first team since the 1998 to 2000 New York Yankees to win three consecutive World Series titles, the league will surely use that data point in its pitch that only a salary cap can save the sport.
And if the Brewers or Rays win their first Series, or if the Guardians win their first since 1948? The league will consider it an aberration, a single-season outcome that means little when compared with the larger sample size of the previous 10 seasons. An exception that proves the rule.
But let's broaden the discussion.
By emphasizing postseason results, the league is devaluing the most accurate measure of a club, the six-month grind of the regular season. Not to mention devaluing the 162 games of inventory all 30 clubs must sell.
Since 2015 -- the line of demarcation the league has set with the Royals' World Series triumph -- the Guardians rank fourth in regular-season wins, the Brewers fifth and the Rays seventh. They are models for other small-market teams, proof that those clubs do not have to operate without hope.
It's true none of those teams won a World Series in the past 10 years. But the Rays got there in the shortened 2020 season. The Guardians reached the American League Championship Series in 2024, the Brewers in 2025. Inferior depth, resulting in part from lower payrolls, might be part of the reason none went further. Adjustments to the collective bargaining agreement could help address that.
No reasonable person would start a league from scratch and adopt baseball's current economic system, in which the league says that the top four spenders -- the Dodgers, New York Mets, Yankees and Philadelphia Phillies -- outspent the bottom 22 in free agency over the course of the current labor agreement.
Reasonable people can disagree, however, whether a cap is the only possible solution when the players' historic opposition to the concept might lead to the cancellation of part or all of the 2027 season.
The league keeps referencing polls saying fans want a cap. Fans, though, evidently are not too upset with the current state of affairs: The league's attendance increased again this year, reaching its highest level since 2016.
Even in cap sports, not every team begins every season with the expectation of competing for a title. The most successful franchises are the shrewdest. Part of baseball's problem is that innovative small-market clubs no longer hold the competitive advantage they once did over less forward-thinking opponents.
Ex // Top Stories
Some of the large-market teams plucked top small-market executives. Very few clubs, if any, continue to lag behind in the intellectual arms race. Even the Colorado Rockies and Washington Nationals, two of the slowest clubs to adapt to baseball's information age, have gotten smarter.
If everyone is essentially working off the same data, payrolls become more of a separator. But even then, the edge money provides is not an absolute guarantee of success in October.
Before winning in the shortened 2020 season, the Dodgers had not won a World Series since 1988. The Mets have not won since 1986. The Phillies and Yankees are experiencing championship droughts that began in 2008 and 2009.
Many baseball executives consider the postseason a crapshoot, fearing the random outcomes that occur in small samples.
The Dodgers, without question, have inordinate financial advantages, including the right to withhold a healthy portion of their massive local TV deal from revenue sharing, a benefit that arose from a settlement the league reached in bankruptcy court with the team's former owner Frank McCourt.
Still, the Dodgers in 2022 and 2023 were eliminated in the division series by rivals from smaller markets, the San Diego Padres and Arizona Diamondbacks. In 2024, the Dodgers' first year with Shohei Ohtani, they nearly lost to the Padres again in division series play. And if not for a series of fortuitous events, they would have lost the 2025 World Series to the Toronto Blue Jays.
Another thing lost in the discussion about the Dodgers' dominance is that villains are good for business. This is the third consecutive season the Dodgers led the majors in road attendance. Their spending forces other NL clubs to try to keep pace. The small-market Padres, in particular, are better for it.
Yet the ability to spend is sometimes a double-edged sword. Long-term contracts sometimes backfire. Seemingly capable of papering over any mistake by simply printing more money, the Dodgers roll merrily along even when free-agent additions such as Kyle Tucker, Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott slump. But several of the Dodgers' biggest and most expensive stars are facing age-related decline. A number of other top-10 payroll clubs, including the Padres, are locked into the same kinds of players.
None of that means that the league and union should proceed as if all is well, assuming the game's cyclical nature will balance things out. The concerns of the small-market clubs must be addressed, and the union acknowledged as much in May with its initial proposals, some of which addressed revenue disparity.
The union proposed enhanced revenue sharing that included protections "to ensure clubs prioritize winning over profiteering"; financial rewards for successful revenue-sharing recipients and draft-pick incentives for them to sign free agents and retain their own players on the verge of hitting the open market.
The league scoffed at the union proposals, as one might expect with the collective bargaining agreement months away from expiration and the parties holding completely different worldviews. Finding a middle ground will be tricky. At least to this point, large-market clubs are willing to share more revenue -- and yield their inherent financial advantages -- but only under a cap system that fixes their costs.
Teams like the Brewers, Rays and Guardians clearly do not require more money to win regular-season games. But the way they operate, frequently trading stars as they get closer to free agency, is far from fan-friendly. Brewers fans buying a Jacob Misiorowski jersey and Rays fans buying a Junior Caminero jersey know not to get too attached to those players. As one small-market executive says: "Championships are won with talent, continuity and experience. We can get talent. The other two are tough to come by."
Tough, but not impossible. Countless examples exist of revenue-sharing recipients signing homegrown players for the long term. The Brewers did it with Jackson Chourio, Cooper Pratt and Luis Lara, the Guardians with José Ramírez and Tanner Bibee. The Pittsburgh Pirates might not keep Paul Skenes, but they locked up Konnor Griffin. The Royals secured extensions with Bobby Witt Jr. and Maikel Garcia, the Seattle Mariners with Cal Raleigh and Julio Rodríguez, the Arizona Diamondbacks with Corbin Carroll and Geraldo Perdomo.
Based on its proposals, the union thinks giving small-market teams an even better opportunity to retain players would benefit the sport. A salary cap is not necessary to make those adjustments and others to the collective bargaining agreement. Much as the league would like fans to believe otherwise, this is not an all-or-nothing situation.
In June, a reporter asked Manfred why he portrays a league he described in 2024 as having a "darn good" record on competitive balance to be out of whack just two years later.
"In the context, particularly of the postseason, where you're trying to generate interest and maximize viewership, I think it's important to emphasize competitiveness," Manfred said. "And there are aspects of competitiveness."
He added: "When we think about it from a labor perspective, we're focused on an entirely different part of the calendar. And that's the offseason, when you're trying to sell season tickets, and the perception among our fans that's really strong that we have a lack of competitiveness."
Maximizing viewership in the postseason? Viewership in the United States last year was the sport's highest since 2017. Selling season tickets? Sure, it's a problem in markets where team owners do not adequately invest in their franchises. It should be less of a problem in places like Milwaukee, Tampa Bay and Cleveland, if we're just talking about the product.
Make the current system fairer, and those clubs will stand even better chances of reaching a postseason that the league expanded to 12 teams from 10 in 2022. Give those clubs enough cracks at the postseason, and eventually one or more will break through.
It could happen this year, if the Brewers, Rays or Guardians win the World Series. The system needs improvement, no doubt. But if competitive balance is the object, it's a lot closer than it appears.

item.title: [MLB.com] Sale looks to 'harness the energy' in Braves postseason debut
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman
item.description: ATLANTA -- When Walt Weiss sends Chris Sale to the mound for Game 1 of the National League Wild Card Series on Tuesday afternoon, he’ll have the same confidence he possessed more than a quarter of a century ago, when he was playing behind John Smoltz, Tom Glavine and Greg Maddux in postseason games. “There’s a different feeling when a guy like that is taking the mound,” Weiss said. “We felt it those years with the Big Three, and I felt it at other times in my career. I felt it in Oakland with Da
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA -- When Walt Weiss sends Chris Sale to the mound for Game 1 of the National League Wild Card Series on Tuesday afternoon, he’ll have the same confidence he possessed more than a quarter of a century ago, when he was playing behind John Smoltz, Tom Glavine and Greg Maddux in postseason games.
“There’s a different feeling when a guy like that is taking the mound,” Weiss said. “We felt it those years with the Big Three, and I felt it at other times in my career. I felt it in Oakland with Dave Stewart. I think it elevates the room the day that guy is pitching.”
Weiss made three straight trips to the playoffs as Atlanta’s shortstop from 1998-2000, and he’s experienced the postseason seven of the past eight years as the team’s bench coach. So, Braves playoff baseball is nothing new for him.
But, for Sale, this will be an experience he has long awaited.
The 37-year-old left-hander’s back prevented him from pitching in the postseason during his 2024 NL Cy Young Award season. But the splendid year he has produced during this third season with Atlanta will be enriched when he throws the first pitch of this Wild Card Series against the Phillies on Tuesday at 2 p.m. ET (NBC/Peacock).
“I love pitching here in Atlanta,” Sale said. “I love pitching in front of these fans, and being able to do it in the postseason makes it that much more special.”
Sale’s greatest postseason moment occurred when he concluded the 2018 World Series for the Red Sox by striking out each of the three batters he faced in the ninth inning of Game 5. His most recent playoff experience occurred in 2021, when, two months after returning from Tommy John surgery, he made three frustrating starts for Boston.
Five years later, Sale is in a far different position. After injuries limited him to a total of 151 innings from 2020-23, the Red Sox essentially gave up on him and sent him to Atlanta prior to the 2024 season. The lanky lefty flourished that year, and has continued to get better. The 2.16 ERA he produced this year ranked third in MLB, and it stands as the fifth-best mark produced by any Braves pitcher who has made at least 25 starts in any season going back to 1920.
So, there truly is reason to think this year’s postseason experience might be different. Sale has constructed a 7.24 ERA in seven previous playoff starts. His struggles weren’t restricted to the 2021 experience. He posted a 6.87 ERA in the four postseason starts he made in 2017 and ‘18. He allowed seven earned runs in one and lasted fewer than five innings in two others.
“I think you learn that it's just about harnessing the energy,” Sale said. “I learned this from David Tollett, my college coach [at Florida Gulf Coast University] -- you can't be better than you are. You can't play above what you possess, and sometimes you go out there and try to do too much, and actually do less.”
The opponents and pitching matchups Sale drew over the past two months prepared him for what he could encounter over the next few weeks. While posting a 2.36 ERA over his final seven starts, he pitched against four playoff teams (Yankees, Brewers, Dodgers and twice against the Phillies) and one (D-backs) that nearly made the postseason.
Within this same stretch, Sale matched up against top-flight starters Gerrit Cole, Jacob Misiorowski, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Cristopher Sánchez and Aaron Nola.
“He’s been nothing short of amazing for us,” Braves first baseman Matt Olson said. “I wouldn’t want anybody else taking the mound for us tomorrow.”
Sale certainly has reason to enter this assignment with confidence. He posted a 2.08 ERA in four starts against the Phillies this season, and the Braves won each of those contests.
If he can garner similar results on Tuesday, there’s a good chance this won’t be the only postseason start he will make this year.
“He presents a whole set of problems, but we've seen him a [few times],” Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said. “We haven't been great with him, but we'll see. Tomorrow is a new day.”
